title: Finding Your Nearest Clinic or Hospital
keyPoints: Public primary healthcare (PHC) clinics are the front door to care: free treatment, no appointment needed in most cases, open on weekdays

Ways to find the nearest facility: ask at any pharmacy or school; ask neighbours and community health workers (CHWs) who do household visits; provincial health departments publish facility lists on their websites; local ward councillors and municipalities keep facility information
Clinics are for most health needs; district hospitals handle emergencies, childbirth, and cases the clinic refers
Bring the ID book or card and, for children, the Road-to-Health Booklet (clinic card); any previous clinic card or file speeds things up
Mobile clinics serve farms and villages on scheduled days — the local clinic or CHW knows the timetable
practicalTips: Arrive early in the morning — files and queues are handled on a first-come basis at most clinics
Every visit, ask for the file to be kept safe; clinics store patient files, so simply return to the same clinic
source: SA National Department of Health / provincial health departments

title: Levels of Care — From Clinic to Tertiary Hospital
keyPoints: Primary level: clinics, community health centres (CHCs) and mobile clinics — everyday illnesses, chronic care, antenatal care, immunisations, minor injuries
District hospital: 24-hour emergency care, maternity, X-rays, and management of conditions beyond the clinic, serving the local district
Regional hospital: specialist services (physicians, surgeons, paediatricians, gynaecologists) receiving referrals from several district hospitals
Tertiary and central hospitals: highly specialised services such as heart surgery, cancer treatment and neurosurgery, linked to medical schools
Each level exists so that complex problems get specialist eyes and simple problems stay close to home
Care should normally start at the clinic — arriving at a tertiary hospital with a minor problem usually means a long wait and a redirect
practicalTips: Emergencies go to the nearest facility that is open — call 10177 and the ambulance will take the patient to the right level of care
Specialist care in the public sector requires a referral letter, except in emergencies

title: The Referral Pathway — How It Works
keyPoints: A referral is a letter from a health worker to a higher level of care explaining the problem, what has been done, and what is needed next
Typical path: clinic nurse or doctor assesses, refers to district hospital; if more specialised care is needed, onward referral to regional or tertiary services
The referral letter is important — keep a copy, bring it to the appointment, and keep it afterwards
Appointment letters state date, time and place; missing a specialist appointment can mean waiting months again — if it cannot be kept, phone or visit the clinic to rearrange
After specialist treatment, patients are usually 'down-referred' back to the local clinic for ongoing medicine and monitoring, which is the intended design, not a downgrade in care
practicalTips: Bring the ID, referral letter, medicines or a list of them, and any test results to every referral appointment
Patient transport is limited — provinces run patient transport for scheduled specialist visits; ask the clinic social worker what is available

title: What Is Free at Public Clinics
keyPoints: Free primary healthcare services at public clinics include: consultations with nurses and doctors, medicines from the clinic formulary, HIV testing and treatment, TB testing and treatment, antenatal and postnatal care, immunisations, family planning, and treatment of ordinary illnesses
Free for everyone at PHC level: this has been national policy since 1996, regardless of income or documentation status
District hospitals charge income-related fees (Uniform Patient Fee System), but those referred by a clinic, pensioners, children, and social-grant recipients are largely exempt
Emergency treatment at any public facility may not be refused while awaiting payment ability
practicalTips: Take proof of income (payslip or affidavit of unemployment) and ID to hospital visits for correct fee assessment
If charged incorrectly after a clinic referral, ask the fees office about the referral exemption
source: SA NDoH / Uniform Patient Fee System / National Health Act

title: Chronic Medication — CCMDD Pick-Up Points
keyPoints: CCMDD (Central Chronic Medicines Dispensing and Distribution), also called Dablapmpa, lets stable chronic patients collect repeat medicines without joining the clinic queue

How it works: the clinic registers a stable patient (on treatment for conditions like HIV, TB, diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy); medicines are packed and delivered to a chosen pick-up point — the clinic's chronic queue, a private pharmacy, a shop, a spaza, or community collection point
Collection is every one to three months, at a chosen date and time; an SMS reminder is usually sent
Adherence clubs — groups collecting together with a quick health check — are an option for stable ART patients
Eligibility is decided by the clinic based on stable condition and controlled readings; ask the nurse at the next visit how to register
practicalTips: Choose a pick-up point that is genuinely easy to reach; it can be changed
Collection is still a clinical visit in miniature — blood pressure or viral load checks happen at set intervals
If medicine runs out before the next collection date, go to the clinic: never just stop chronic medication

title: Getting Repeat Chronic Medication at the Clinic
keyPoints: Stable chronic patients receive medicines in 2-3 month supplies at clinic chronic-care visits
A follow-up date is given at each visit — the file, scripts and stock are prepared around that date
Blood tests (for example viral load, HbA1c, kidney tests) are scheduled at intervals; missing visits delays these checks
If treatment is started privately or in another province, bring the boxes or a letter — the clinic can continue the same regimen if it is on the formulary
practicalTips: Collect the next supply in the final week of the current one — never wait until the last tablet
Never share chronic medication with family or neighbours, even with the same condition — doses are individual
When travelling or moving, ask the clinic for a transfer letter to a new facility

title: National Health Insurance (NHI) — What It Means
keyPoints: NHI is South Africa's plan for universal health coverage: a single fund that pays for healthcare for everyone, based on need rather than ability to pay
The NHI Act was signed into law in May 2024; implementation is phased over many years and pilot activities are underway
The goal is that services at clinics and hospitals are covered by the fund, ending out-of-pocket payments for care at registered providers
During the transition, public services continue exactly as they work today — free PHC services, clinic-first referrals, CCMDD — and medical aid continues to exist alongside
Practical meaning for households today: the public system's free and subsidised services are the baseline; NHI will formalise and expand this over time
practicalTips: For now, nothing changes about how the clinic is used — register at the local clinic as normal
Official information comes from the National Department of Health; be cautious of scams selling 'NHI registration' — there is no fee and no card to buy
source: SA NDoH / National Health Insurance Act 20 of 2023

title: Patient Rights and Responsibilities
keyPoints: The Patient Rights Charter is national policy: every person has the right to access healthcare, including emergency care, reproductive health services, and confidentiality
Right to respect and dignity: care without discrimination on any grounds — race, gender, age, disability, sexual orientation, nationality or HIV status
Right to information: what is wrong, what treatment is proposed, what it involves, and the right to refuse treatment after being informed of the consequences
Right to privacy and confidentiality: health information stays confidential; HIV status cannot be disclosed to others without consent
Right to participate in decisions: including the right to a second opinion and to know the identity of the person providing care
Responsibilities: to give accurate information, to follow agreed treatment, to respect health workers and other patients, and to use health services responsibly (emergencies lines for emergencies)
practicalTips: A named point of complaint exists at every facility — ask for the person in charge or the quality assurance officer
Unresolved complaints can be lodged with the Office of Health Standards Compliance (see sahs-012)

title: Emergency Numbers and When to Use Them
keyPoints: 10177 — national ambulance / emergency medical services
112 — works from any cellphone, free, even with no airtime; connects to emergency services
10111 — police emergency; for violence, danger and crime scenes
0861 555 777 — Poisons Information Helpline for swallowed medicines, chemicals, paraffin and pesticides

Call the ambulance for: unresponsiveness, trouble breathing, chest pain, stroke signs (face droop, arm weakness, speech trouble), heavy bleeding, seizures, poisoning, serious injuries, and any maternity emergency
When calling: give the exact location (street, landmark), what happened, how many people are hurt, and a callback number; stay on the line until told to hang up
practicalTips: While waiting for an ambulance: unlock the gate and doors, put on outside lights at night, send someone to the road to direct the crew, and gather medicines and documents
If transport to hospital is faster than waiting for an ambulance in a life-threatening emergency, do not delay — get to the nearest facility

title: Making the Most of a Clinic Visit
keyPoints: Arrive early: most clinics open around 07:00 and queues for files and triage form quickly
Bring: ID or birth certificate, child's Road-to-Health Booklet, previous clinic card, a list of all medicines being taken, and cash or a card for transport home
Write down symptoms and questions before the visit — a short list means nothing important is forgotten in a busy consultation
Ask the nurse or doctor to explain the diagnosis, the medicine, and when to come back — it is a right to understand
Find out the clinic's chronic-illness day and antenatal day — separate queues for these move faster
practicalTips: Take a snack and water; clinic days can be long, especially for diabetics on medication
Ask a family member or friend to come along when the visit involves a lot of information or a new diagnosis
Community health workers attached to the clinic can follow up at home — ask how to reach them
source: SA NDoH / provincial health department guidance

title: Sick Notes and Medical Certificates
keyPoints: A medical certificate (sick note) is issued by a registered health professional authorised to diagnose — a doctor, or a nurse with prescribing and diagnisory authority within primary healthcare
Ask for the certificate during the visit itself; it should state that the person was examined and found unfit for work, and for how long
Under the Basic Conditions of Employment Act, an employer may require a certificate for absences of more than two consecutive days (or twice in eight weeks, depending on the agreement)
Backdating: certificates can state that the person was examined on that day and reports being ill since an earlier date; honest communication with the employer is best
Certificates are medical documents — forged or bought sick notes are fraud
practicalTips: Ask the clinic specifically: 'I need a sick note for my employer' before leaving
For chronic conditions requiring work adjustments (for example heavy lifting), ask the clinic to document it in a letter
source: Basic Conditions of Employment Act / HPCSA guidance

title: Complaints About Health Services
keyPoints: First step: raise the problem with the facility manager or the person in charge of the clinic or ward — many problems are solved on the spot
Step two: provincial health departments have complaints lines and offices; the complaint is escalated with the facility name, date, and what happened
The Office of Health Standards Compliance (OHSC) is the national watchdog for both public and private facilities: it inspects facilities and can investigate unresolved complaints of poor quality care
OHSC complaints call centre: toll-free 080 911 6472; email complaints@ohsc.org.za; complaints can also be lodged via the OHSC website
Complaints about health professionals' conduct go to their professional councils; complaints about private healthcare costs go to the Council for Medical Schemes (for scheme members)
practicalTips: Write down dates, names, and what was said while it is fresh — specific complaints are acted on faster
Whistleblowers reporting in good faith are protected; the OHSC keeps complainants' details confidential where requested
source: Office of Health Standards Compliance / National Health Amendment Act

title: Traditional Healers and the Health System
keyPoints: Traditional healers are an established part of health-seeking for many South African households, and the majority of the population consults them at some point

Some combinations are safe in parallel care, but interactions are real: certain herbal remedies reduce antiretroviral (ARV) levels, affect epilepsy medicines, or stress the liver alongside TB treatment
Tell the clinic nurse or doctor what traditional or herbal medicines are being used — this is confidential information used for safety, and good health workers will not judge or scold
Never stop prescribed chronic medication (ART, TB treatment, epilepsy or diabetes medicines) in favour of an alternative without discussing it with the clinic
Traditional health practitioners are being formally integrated into the national health system, including collaboration on notifiable conditions
practicalTips: If a healer advises stopping clinic medicine, ask the clinic for a joint plan before stopping anything
Bring the containers of all remedies being used to the clinic visit — names alone are often not enough
source: SA NDoH Traditional Health Practitioners framework / WHO

title: Medical Aid and Using Public Services
keyPoints: Medical aid (health insurance) is private cover; public clinics and hospitals are separate and generally used by those without cover — public services do not require medical aid
Public hospital fees are income-related for those who can pay; medical aid members treated in public hospitals are billed accordingly
Prescribed Minimum Benefits (PMBs): medical schemes must cover a defined list of conditions — including HIV, TB and many chronic conditions — in full, regardless of the plan type
Chronic patients on medical aid should register their condition with the scheme for chronic medicine benefits
practicalTips: Keep the medical aid card and ID together for private visits
Even with medical aid, emergency public sector care is available when needed; inform the scheme afterwards
For scheme disputes or refused PMB claims, the Council for Medical Schemes (0861 123 267) assists
source: Council for Medical Schemes / Medical Schemes Act
